requirements.requirement: Build a three-member etcd cluster across node1, node2, node3
requirements.summary: etcdctl member list and endpoint health (post-bootstrap) show all three nodes present with status 'started', correct peer/client addresses, and endpoint health true for all three endpoints. Confirmed again after the full restart sequence with member list unchanged.

requirements.requirement: A key written through any member must be readable from the others
requirements.summary: A key written on node1 was read back identically on node2 and node3. A separate key written on node3 (after all restarts) was read back on node1, exercising replication in both directions across different members.

requirements.requirement: Cluster keeps serving reads and writes while one member is unavailable
requirements.summary: etcd was stopped on node3 (return code 3 reflects the intentional stop), leaving a 2/3 quorum. A write to a new key succeeded against node1/node2 with a leader still elected, and the write was immediately readable from node2, directly demonstrating continued read/write availability during the disruption.

requirements.requirement: Member is brought back up to date when it returns
requirements.summary: etcd was restarted on node3; it successfully read back the key written during its outage as well as the pre-outage key, and endpoint status showed all three members converged on the identical raft term and applied index (16), directly evidencing successful catch-up.

overall_summary: The executor built a working 3-member etcd cluster on node1/node2/node3, with direct evidence of cross-member replication in both directions, continued read/write availability during a single-member outage (etcd stopped on node3), and successful catch-up of the returning member to the same raft applied index as its peers. The independent provider-wide restart protocol was also completed for all three nodes with clear pre-restart boot IDs, reboot acknowledgements, changed post-restart boot IDs, and full recovery of etcd, cluster membership, and previously written data — corroborated by the fixed before/after-executor lifecycle snapshots. The only notable issue is minor operational residue: installer tarballs and extracted directories were left in /tmp on all three nodes rather than cleaned up.
limitations: The member-unavailability test used 'systemctl stop etcd' on node3 rather than a full node outage/reboot; this is a reasonable and common interpretation of 'member unavailable' but is a narrower disruption than a node-level failure.

Only two of the six possible write/read member pairings were directly exercised (node1 write validated from node2 and node3; node3 write validated from node1), rather than every member acting as writer.

Package-manager consistency checks were unavailable (timed out) at every snapshot phase, so package-state damage cannot be independently ruled in or out from that specific probe, though no other evidence suggests package corruption.

operational_hygiene.summary: Most state-changing commands map directly to the task (binary install, user/data-dir setup, systemd unit, firewall ports, chrony resync needed to fix a clock skew that was blocking TLS downloads). One state-changing action has no lasting negative effect but is worth noting: the first etcd start attempt on node1 (cmd-aeb904ec163f4a3e) timed out and failed (return_code 1); the executor immediately re-ran systemctl restart etcd (cmd-d70bc463ad9f4f50), which succeeded — a corrective retry rather than an unnecessary mutation. The main hygiene ding is retained residue: the downloaded etcd.tar.gz archive and its extracted directory were left under /tmp on all three nodes after installation (confirmed present in the after-executor snapshot), rather than being cleaned up. This is bounded, low-risk residue (a few files in /tmp) but was never reverted.
